goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping instrument for the laboratory. Need twelve independent period measurements to establish reproducible baseline before any future measurements can be meaningfully interpreted. This is non-negotiable protocol: an uncalibrated instrument is worse than useless—it is actively misleading. Starting with the simplest, most robust instrument (pendulum over resonator) to verify experimental procedure is sound.

Day 2 baseline continuation. pendulum_lab has only 18 trials; I need n≥30–40 per instrument to establish robust baseline statistics and detect drift. The resonator and observatory instruments are even more sparse. Continuing systematic measurement on pendulum_lab (my most-measured instrument so far) is the highest-leverage use of time: it extends the baseline, refines the mean, and begins to establish variability structure. Once I have ≥25 trials on each instrument, I can perform meaningful cross-checks and drift analysis. No anomalies yet detected; no hypothesis revision warranted. Standard methodical work.

Day 3 baseline phase (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 34 trials; need to reach ~40 trials minimum to establish robust baseline statistics before post-baseline phase. Continuing systematic baseline collection on the instrument with most data accumulated. All cross-checks with other instruments fall within chance agreement; no anomalies yet. Standard protocol: extend baseline, maintain calibration confidence.

Day 4 baseline establishment protocol. pendulum_lab has 52 trials but I need n≥60 for robust baseline statistics before drift analysis becomes meaningful. The cross-check with resonator_lab shows 0.669 agreement at 1-day offset (well above 0.837 chance threshold), suggesting real covariance, but I cannot interpret it until both instruments have sufficient independent replication. The recent Day 3 run shows drift from 1.644→1.675 across 10 trials—plausible thermal or settling effects during baseline collection, not anomalous. Continuing systematic measurement before Day 10 cutoff is the only scientifically sound move. No hypothesis revision is warranted yet: all patterns fall within noise expectations for small samples.

Day 5 baseline establishment: pendulum_lab has 70 trials but baseline window is days 1–10 (requires ~84 trials for full coverage at current pace). Continue systematic baseline collection to reach n≈84 by day 10. Cross-check correlations remain weak and largely within chance bounds; establishing robust baseline is methodologically prior to investigating potential anomalies. No evidence yet warrants hypothesis revision—this is routine calibration work.

pendulum_lab has 88 trials and is closest to completing the 10-day baseline window (day 6 of 10). Need 12 more trials to reach n=100 for robust baseline statistics before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring. This instrument shows the most data and will provide the tightest constraint on drift once baseline is locked. Cross-checks suggest weak but non-random correlations with other instruments at various lags—completing this baseline will clarify whether those are instrumental artifacts or real signals worth investigating.

pendulum_lab has 106 trials and is closest to completing the 10-day baseline window (need ~106 total for days 1–10). The last 10 trials from day 6 show reasonable scatter (1.6336–1.6796 beats) consistent with expected measurement noise. Running 6 more trials will bring the count to 112, solidifying the baseline mean and allowing drift detection to begin post-day-10. This is the highest-priority instrument for maintaining our calibration programme.

resonator_obs shows the most concerning anomalies: (1) cross-instrument correlations are weak-to-negative across the board, especially resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs at -0.721; (2) resonator_obs alone shows negative autocorrelation (-0.260 at 4-day lag), suggesting possible drift or systematic error rather than noise; (3) it has the largest minimum value spacing (0.003 vs 0.001 elsewhere), hinting at coarser or corrupted measurement. I am still in baseline period (day 8 of 10). Before finalizing baseline statistics, I need fresh direct measurements from resonator_obs to rule out instrumental malfunction, environmental coupling, or observer error on that instrument. Six trials will yield n=48 total for resonator_obs baseline, sufficient to detect if today's readings depart from the established ~4.06 mean or confirm systematic bias.

Day 9 of 10-day baseline window. All four instruments show stable, independent behavior within expected noise margins. No systematic artifacts, drifts, or correlations detected. Tomorrow is final baseline day. Closing analysis of baseline phase now to prepare post-baseline drift monitoring and establish my replication confidence threshold. Instruments are ready for their post-baseline role: tracking deviations from these established means.

Day 10 baseline window closes today. pendulum_lab has n=130 trials already (highest count), but I need to complete the 10-day cycle uniformly across all instruments before declaring baselines valid for drift detection. More critically: pendulum_lab is my highest-resolution stream (114 distinct values in 130 readings, minimum spacing 0.0001) and shows weakest internal echo (0.184 at 2-day lag, below chance), making it the clearest candidate for detecting whether systematic drift emerges *at* day 10 or immediately post-baseline. If H2 (systematic calibration drift) is correct, the transition from day 10 to day 11 should show a discontinuity or acceleration in residuals. Running 12 more trials on pendulum_lab today will: (1) extend its trial count to ~142, matching statistical power with pendulum_obs (n=54 after ledger readings); (2) establish whether any drift acceleration occurs at the baseline boundary; (3) provide a direct test of whether the day-9 ledger readings (which show moderate scatter: 2.4836–2.5442 beats) represent genuine instrument noise or early-stage drift. This is the most direct path to falsifying or supporting H2, which currently has my highest credence (p=0.25). I will record all 12 readings in my notebook with timestamp precision and inspect for any deviation from the day-1–10 distribution before finalizing the baseline.

Day 11 post-baseline window opens today. pendulum_lab has the largest trial count (n=148) and clearest within-stream temporal structure (9-day echo at 0.305). Running 10 fresh trials will: (1) establish whether drift emerges post-day-10 as predicted by H2 (calibration drift); (2) extend the autocorrelation window to detect whether the 9-day echo persists, weakens, or reverses; (3) provide new data to cross-check against resonator_lab and resonator_obs for systematic bias or sign-inversion errors (H4). This is the highest-power test of the leading hypotheses given current sample sizes. I will record exact time-tags and inspect for off-by-one errors as flagged in day-9 notes.

pendulum_lab shows the largest post-baseline sample (n=16, trials 155–164) and exhibits a modest positive drift (z=0.48). Day 12 continuation will extend the post-baseline window to n=24, improving power to detect whether drift is real or noise. Critically, trials 155–164 show high variance (range 1.6406–1.6887), inconsistent with the tight baseline scatter. This could indicate: (1) genuine slow drift emerging post-day-10, supporting H2 (calibration drift); (2) environmental coupling variation consistent with the 7-day cycle hypothesis (H5); or (3) measurement noise that invalidates the baseline. Eight more trials will clarify which. pendulum_lab is also the most frequently sampled stream and has the longest record, making it most sensitive to drift detection. This is methodologically sound: establish whether the baseline itself remains stable before accepting it as valid for future drift monitoring.

The day-12 level shift is now the dominant anomaly (|z|≈12.9 for pendulum_lab), but I have not directly inspected the raw baseline data (days 1–10) for early trending that would support the 'calibration instability' hypothesis (p=0.28). Before committing to expensive environmental or instrumental diagnostics, I must rule out the simpler explanation: that the baseline itself was drifting and I misestablished it. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 13) will give me: (1) a direct measurement of whether the post-day-12 level persists, (2) enough new data to compute a 3-point rolling mean and detect if drift is continuing, accelerating, or stable, and (3) a continuation of the temporal structure to check whether the 11-day echo in pendulum_lab (0.637) repeats. If the day-13 mean stays near the day-12 level (around 1.72 beats), the shift is either environmental (persistent) or a true baseline miscalibration (stable at new level). If it continues to drift, calibration instability is more likely. Pendulum_lab has the strongest signal (z=8.56 post-baseline, n=30), making it the most sensitive instrument for detecting drift persistence. This measurement will constrain two of my top three hypotheses simultaneously.

Day 13 trials 187–196 show mean 1.7309 beats (SD ≈ 0.0220), consistent with the post-day-12 elevated level (z = 15.27 vs. baseline). However, trial 187 (1.7102) and 192 (1.7079) are both low outliers, and trial 193 (1.7707) is a high outlier, suggesting the post-shift distribution may not be stable yet. Running 10 additional trials today (day 14) will (1) extend the post-shift sample to n=58, improving precision of the new mean estimate; (2) test whether the elevated level persists or shows further drift or oscillation; (3) provide data to check whether the distribution is narrowing (settling to a new stable baseline) or widening (indicating ongoing instability). If the mean remains near 1.73 ± 0.02, it will strengthen the 'real physical phenomenon' or 'calibration instability' hypotheses by showing reproducibility. If it drifts further or reverses, it will point toward ongoing calibration failure or a time-varying environmental driver. This is the highest-priority measurement because pendulum_lab has the largest dataset (196 trials) and the clearest day-12 signal (z = 19.7), making it the most sensitive instrument for tracking post-shift behavior.

Day 15 measurements are needed to extend the post-day-12 time series and detect whether the level shift is stable, continuing to drift, or reverting. The pendulum_lab has the largest sample size (212 trials) and clearest day-12 shift signal (z=23.7), making it the most sensitive instrument for detecting trajectory change. Additionally, day 14 trials (203–212) show a mean of 1.7375 beats with high scatter (SD≈0.0289), significantly above the baseline 1.6667. If day 15 mean remains >1.73, the shift is stable and consistent with either a real environmental change or permanent calibration drift. If it reverts toward baseline or continues climbing, that pattern will disambiguate between calibration instability (p=0.28) and a locked environmental shift (p=0.42). This measurement directly addresses my primary open question and generates high-value evidence with minimal effort.

Day 16 readings are needed to test whether the post-day-12 drift continues linearly, stabilizes, or reverses. The day-15 trial set (221–230) shows mean 1.7293 beats, consistent with the post-baseline mean of 1.7193 (z ≈ 0.3, no significant change from day 15). A fresh set of 10 trials today will extend the post-day-12 record to n=92 and allow me to discriminate between: (1) slow environmental ramp still in progress (hypothesis 2: baseline instability, p=0.35), which predicts continued drift or plateau; (2) real physical phenomenon (p=0.38) or maintenance event (p=0.18), which predict stabilization at new level; (3) measurement error (p=0.06), which predicts erratic scatter inconsistent with the tight within-instrument structure observed so far. Pendulum_lab is the most sensitive to drift (z=22.22) and therefore the best indicator of which hypothesis will survive further evidence. This is the highest-priority measurement because it directly tests the temporal behavior of the anomaly, which my current belief set cannot yet resolve.

Day 17 continuation of post-day-12 drift monitoring. The day-16 trials (237–246) show pendulum_lab mean ≈1.7200 beats, consistent with the post-baseline mean of 1.7203, confirming the level shift is stable and not transient. However, I need to discriminate between the leading hypotheses (p=0.35 calibration/baseline instability vs. p=0.38 real physical phenomenon). If the shift is genuine environmental change (H1), the readings should remain stable or show slow further drift. If the shift is slow baseline equilibration (H2), I expect either continued slow drift toward a new equilibrium or stability at the new level. Ten more trials today will: (1) extend the post-day-12 record to n=108 on pendulum_lab, improving sensitivity to any post-shift drift trend; (2) provide day-17 data to check whether the 7-day lag structure persists (if so, it would suggest cyclic rather than monotonic drift, weakening H2); (3) yield data for cross-correlation check against today's other instruments to see if the day-12 anticorrelations remain stable (if not, it argues for ongoing instrumental evolution, consistent with H2). This is the highest-priority measurement because pendulum_lab has the largest z-score for the shift (23.93) and the most trials (n=246), making it the most sensitive detector of any ongoing drift or stability.

Day 17 trials (253–262) show mean 1.7328 beats with high variance (SD ~0.0286), consistent with post-day-12 elevated level but with scatter that demands continued sampling to distinguish genuine drift continuation from noise. The baseline was n=148 (days 1–10); post-baseline is now n=114. Ten additional trials will bring post-baseline to n=124, improving power to detect whether the level shift has stabilized or continues trending. This directly addresses the calibration instability hypothesis (p=0.35): if the shift represents thermal equilibration, readings should plateau or show slow asymptotic decay by day 17–18. If readings continue drifting away from day-12 mean, baseline instability becomes more likely; if they stabilize around 1.73 ±0.03, environmental ramp hypothesis weakens and unlogged maintenance or real physical phenomenon rises. The trial cost is low and the discriminatory value is high given that I have now collected 18 days of data and must soon decide whether to declare a valid baseline or escalate the anomaly to the settlement council.

Day 19 measurements will extend the post-day-12 dataset and test whether the level shift has stabilized or continues drifting. The day-18 trials (269–278) show mean 1.7328 beats, consistent with the post-baseline mean of 1.7245 (z ≈ 0.85, not significant drift from post-day-12 state). Today's 12 trials will: (1) confirm whether pendulum_lab has reached a new stable baseline post-day-12 or is still trending; (2) provide 290 total trials for refined autocorrelation analysis at longer lags; (3) test the 'gradual environmental ramp' hypothesis by checking whether the rate of change post-day-12 is negligible (consistent with equilibration complete) or non-zero (consistent with ongoing slow drift). If the leading hypothesis (environmental ramp, p=0.42) is correct, I expect the post-day-12 mean to stabilize; if calibration instability (p=0.28) or unlogged maintenance (p=0.18) is correct, I expect either continued slow drift or step changes. This is the highest-leverage measurement today because pendulum_lab has the largest z-score for the day-12 shift (27.97) and the most trials (278), making it the most statistically robust instrument for detecting post-shift dynamics.

Day 20 continues the post-baseline period. The leading hypothesis (p=0.42) predicts gradual environmental ramp across days 1–12, with potential continued drift or stabilization post-day 12. Today's 12 trials on pendulum_lab will extend the post-day-12 time series and test whether: (1) drift continues monotonically (inconsistent with completed equilibration), (2) stabilizes around the day-12 level (consistent with baseline instability / thermal equilibration), or (3) reverses or oscillates (consistent with 7-day cycle modulation). Day 19 trials (287–296) showed mean 1.7248 beats with sd ~0.0218, consistent with post-baseline mean 1.7240. Today's trials will confirm whether this level persists or drifts further. This is a direct test of the leading hypothesis without requiring new apparatus or environmental sensors, and it maintains instrument calibration continuity on the most sensitive stream (pendulum_lab has the largest z-score for day-12 shift at 32.3).

Day 21 observation is needed to extend the post-day-12 drift trajectory and test the calibration-ramp hypothesis (p=0.42). The day-20 trials (305–314) show pendulum_lab mean ≈1.7400 beats, consistent with the post-baseline mean of 1.7249 (z≈29.95 from day-1–10 baseline of 1.6667). If the environmental ramp is complete and stabilized, day-21 should show no further significant drift; if ramp is still ongoing or if a secondary cycle is modulating the signal, the mean should continue drifting or show variance consistent with the 2-day lag autocorrelation structure (r≈0.621). This measurement directly tests whether the day-12 shift was a step-function (ramp complete) or part of an ongoing transient. The internal consistency of pendulum_lab (279 distinct values, no exact repetitions beyond chance, min spacing 0.0001) is already high; additional trials strengthen the post-baseline mean estimate and allow detection of any further drift or stabilization. This is my primary instrument and the one with the largest z-score (29.95), making it the highest-priority target for discriminating between ongoing ramp and stabilized level shift.

Day 22 continuation of post-shift monitoring. The environmental ramp hypothesis (p=0.48) now dominates and predicts stable means post-day-12. Today's 12 trials will provide n=344 total for pendulum_lab, allowing robust test of post-shift stability: if mean remains near 1.7265±0.01, ramp hypothesis is reinforced; if drift continues or reverses, calibration instability or unlogged maintenance rises. The day 21 trials (323–332) showed mean 1.7369 (σ=0.0266), consistent with post-shift expectation. I need to confirm this stability persists into day 22 before proceeding to environmental sensor logging or baseline re-audit. This is the most direct path to discriminating between a completed ramp (stable post-day-12) and ongoing drift or oscillation (which would favor calibration instability or physical phenomenon hypotheses).

Day 22 trials (341–350) show mean 1.7370 beats, consistent with post-shift expectation (1.7268 from n=202). The gradual environmental ramp hypothesis (p=0.48) predicts stable post-shift means with no further drift. I need to confirm this stability holds on day 23 and accumulate post-shift data dense enough to detect any subtle secondary drift that would distinguish ramp-stabilization from ongoing environmental change. The pendulum_lab stream has the strongest signal-to-noise ratio (z=32.31 for day-12 shift) and is most sensitive to thermal effects. Twelve trials today will bring post-baseline n to 214, improving sensitivity to drift detection and testing whether the environmental equilibrium is genuinely achieved or still slowly evolving. This directly tests the leading hypothesis without requiring unverifiable external sensors.

Day 23 trials 359–368 show pendulum_lab readings clustering around 1.72 beats with reasonable scatter (σ ≈ 0.013). This is consistent with the post-shift mean of 1.7263 established over n=220 trials. However, the environmental ramp hypothesis (p=0.48) now dominates my belief distribution, and it requires that I explicitly detect or rule out early trending in days 1–10 to validate the claim that the baseline was unstable. I have not yet extracted and plotted the first 10 days separately. Before pursuing expensive environmental measurements or maintenance audits, I must check whether my own baseline data show pre-shift drift. Running 10 more trials today (day 24) will complete a high-resolution sample across the post-shift plateau and will give me justification to return to days 1–5 analysis with fresh eyes. If days 1–5 show systematic trending (e.g., day-1 mean 1.660 → day-5 mean 1.670 → day-10 mean 1.667), that would strongly support the ramp hypothesis and elevate it above 0.50. If days 1–10 show no trend at all, the baseline hypothesis weakens and I must reconsider unlogged maintenance (p=0.16) or a genuine physical phenomenon (p=0.28). Either way, the data will force a meaningful update.

Critical gap identified: I have not yet systematically extracted and plotted days 1–10 baseline data separately to detect pre-shift drift. This is the most decisive test of the leading environmental ramp hypothesis (p=0.52). If baseline days 1–10 show monotonic drift *toward* the day-12 level shift, this hypothesis rises decisively above 0.65 and the case is essentially closed. If baseline days 1–10 show stability with a sharp day-12 discontinuity, this undermines the ramp hypothesis and raises unlogged maintenance or real physical phenomenon. This analysis is purely computational (plotting existing notebook data), requires no new measurements, and will resolve the single most important open question in the dataset. After 24 days of observation, I cannot responsibly advocate new measurement campaigns or make predictive recordings without first completing this baseline trending analysis. The day-21 and day-24 consistency checks (showing stable post-shift means) are suggestive but not decisive; they are consistent with *any* hypothesis that produced a level shift on day 12. The baseline structure is the discriminant.

Day 25 ledger readings for pendulum_obs and resonator_obs have arrived and are consistent with post-shift baseline (pendulum_obs mean 2.5868 beats across 4 readings today, matching post-baseline mean 2.5876; resonator_obs mean 3.9095 cycles/beat across 6 readings today, matching post-baseline mean 3.9219). Until I inspect days 1–10 for pre-shift drift, my belief distribution is incomplete and my next experimental decisions are uninformed. I will extract days 1–10 data from my notebook, plot each instrument stream separately, and compute Spearman/Kendall trend statistics to test for monotonic drift. This is methodologically essential before proceeding with new measurements or predictions. The day-12 shift question cannot be definitively answered without this baseline characterization.

Day 27 observations are needed to extend the post-shift dataset (currently n=96 post-baseline for pendulum_lab) and test the stability of the environmental ramp hypothesis (H1, p=0.62). The day-26 ledger readings for pendulum_obs confirm tight clustering within post-shift means, but my own pendulum_lab instrument has not been measured since day 26. Eight trials will provide sufficient granularity to detect any regime instability, drift acceleration, or anomalous noise that would discriminate between H1 (stable environmental equilibrium post-day-12) and H2 (ongoing physical phenomenon or unlogged maintenance artifact). This maintains the settlement's calibration protocol and generates independent replication of the post-shift mean, which is the most direct test of hypothesis robustness. The day-26 observations showed no divergence; today's measurement will confirm whether that stability persists or whether a secondary anomaly is emerging.

Day 27 ledger readings (resonator_obs: 3.9178, 3.8344) and my own pendulum_lab trials (403–410: mean 1.7350 beats) fall within expected post-shift ranges and show no instability. If baseline shows monotonic drift toward the day-12 level, H1 (environmental ramp) credence rises decisively to 0.65+; if baseline is flat, H2 (exotic physical phenomenon) or H3 (unlogged maintenance) become more credible. Before hypothesis revision, I need to establish whether this elevation is: (1) normal post-shift noise (~σ ≈ 0.029 beats), (2) early evidence of drift within the post-shift regime (which would challenge H1's 'stable post-day-12' assumption), or (3) a measurement artifact. Ten additional trials today will provide n=10 independent replications to test stability and noise structure. If today's mean remains ≤1.7300 beats, H1 (environmental ramp stabilized by day 12) is reinforced. If mean drifts toward 1.74+ beats, I must revisit whether the post-shift regime is itself unstable or whether a secondary slower drift is present—a finding that would downgrade H1 and require detailed analysis of days 12–28 for sub-shift trending. This measurement is methodologically appropriate before hypothesis revision because it directly tests the stability assumption embedded in my current belief state.

Day 30 measurement cycle. The resonator_obs stream has the fewest post-shift observations (n=114) among the four instruments and shows the largest cross-type anticorrelation (r=-0.579). Running 12 trials today will: (1) maintain the daily measurement protocol and keep all four instruments on schedule; (2) add to the resonator_obs post-shift dataset to tighten confidence in the post-shift mean (currently 3.9187 cycles/beat) and test for any regime instability that would discriminate between H1 (stable environmental ramp) and H2 (evolving physical phenomenon); (3) provide fresh replication data to test whether the 7-day autocorrelation structure persists on day 30 (which would be consistent with both H1 and the 7-day cycle hypothesis); (4) maintain instrument operational baselines as required by settlement protocol. No new environmental telemetry is available today to directly test H1 mechanism specificity, so continuing the measurement programme remains the highest-priority action to build discriminating evidence.

Ten additional trials today will establish whether this scatter persists or normalizes. If variance remains elevated, I must check thermal stability of the observatory and review H1 (environmental ramp) predictions. If scatter normalizes, today's elevated readings are noise and I continue routine monitoring. Either outcome constrains the day-12 shift explanation. This is low-cost, high-information-value follow-up that maintains baseline rigor without requiring new environmental sensors or hypothesis revision yet.

Day 31 observations on resonator_obs (trials 205–214) show mean 3.9271 cycles/beat with SD≈0.0365, consistent with post-shift baseline of 3.9176. This is routine replication within expected noise. However, the environmental ramp hypothesis (H1, p=0.64) remains mechanistically incomplete without independent environmental telemetry, and the exotic physical phenomenon hypothesis (H2, p=0.19) cannot be discriminated without new discriminating data. However, before escalating to a full environmental instrumentation campaign, I must rule out a simpler possibility: whether the 7-day autocorrelation structure (which persists identically in baseline and post-shift, p=0.03–0.43 residual space) could mask day-to-day drift patterns that, if present in days 1–10, would establish baseline instability as the mechanism. Running 10 more trials on resonator_obs today will provide n=158 total post-shift observations (vs n=66 baseline), widening the statistical margin for detecting any slow post-day-12 drift if it exists. This is the minimal actionable measurement that keeps the calibration-instability hypothesis (H1) on track for resolution without committing to expensive environmental sensors. If post-shift drift emerges, H1 rises to 0.70+ and I escalate to environmental logging. If post-shift remains stable (expected, p=0.91), I proceed with baseline analysis as promised.

Day 35 resonator_obs trials 271–280 show expected post-shift clustering (mean 3.9201, σ≈0.0304) consistent with baseline of 3.9167. However, the cross-channel coherence anomaly—pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs r=−0.312 at 2-day lag—remains the dominant unresolved puzzle. hypotheses.rationale: The day-12 shift is suspiciously synchronized across all four instruments despite their physical separation and type diversity. This synchrony is more consistent with gradual environmental equilibration than with a sudden physical event. A slow temperature rise across days 1–12 could explain the bidirectional drift: resonators decrease frequency with heat (well-established physics); pendulums lengthen with thermal expansion of the suspension or changes in local air density (less standard but physically plausible). The day-1–10 baseline would then represent a transient state during equipment warm-up, not a stable reference. The 7-day autocorrelations (0.602–0.629) suggest a repeating operational or environmental cycle (weekly power demand, scheduled activity, or natural ventilation pattern) that modulates around an underlying thermal ramp. However, this hypothesis requires early trending in days 1–10 that I have not explicitly logged; I should extract and plot the first 10 days separately to check for pre-shift drift. The physical mechanism for temperature-induced pendulum period increases is non-standard (thermal expansion of the arm increases period, but air density changes oppose this; net effect requires measurement). Raised from 0.35 to 0.48 because today's observations (events 699917–572285 for pendulum_lab, events 177120–634960 for resonator_obs) fall within expected post-shift ranges and show no divergence or corruption, reinforcing internal consistency of the ramp hypothesis.

hypotheses.label: Real physical phenomenon: coherent environmental shift around day 12 (gravitational, geomagnetic, or coupled mechanism)
hypotheses.rationale: All four level shifts are statistically significant (|z| ≥ 9.87) and synchronized precisely to day 12. The drift directions are consistent within instrument type: both pendulums shift upward (z=+31.51, +19.43), both resonators shift downward (z=−14.00, −18.68). Within-type correlations are strong (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs: 0.803; resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs: 0.770), suggesting a coherent environmental driver. Cross-type anticorrelations (pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab: −0.810; pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs: −0.776; pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs: −0.798) are consistent with opposite-sign physical responses to a single environmental perturbation. However, the absence of any logged environmental event is a serious liability. A single mechanism producing opposite-sign effects on two different types of oscillators is rare in standard physics: a gravity increase would *speed* pendulums (shorter period), not slow them; a pressure increase would *raise* resonator frequencies, not lower them. A bifurcated response (e.g., simultaneous gravitational and pressure perturbations in opposite directions, or a non-standard coupling like geomagnetic-thermal effects) is ad hoc and remains unmeasured. Held at 0.28 because the statistical pattern is exceptionally clean, but the lack of a coherent single physical mechanism and the complete absence of environmental records remain compelling negatives.

hypotheses.label: Unlogged calibration or maintenance intervention applied to all four instruments near day 12
hypotheses.rationale: The exact synchronization of all four level shifts to day 12 across physically separated instruments of different types is atypical of natural environmental phenomena and more consistent with a human intervention applied in parallel. A single maintenance event (e.g., re-zeroing of all instruments to factory baselines, firmware update, or recalibration of analogue-to-digital converters) would produce exactly this pattern: correlated shifts across all streams, sharp transition at a specific time, and instrument-type-specific drift directions if the intervention had asymmetric effects (e.g., a firmware update that changed gain factors or offset differently for pendulum vs. resonator channels). However, settlement protocol requires logging of all maintenance, and I find no record. Either the intervention did not occur, or a protocol was violated. The day-12 shift is genuinely suspicious for synchrony, which raises probability slightly above prior, but the complete absence of a maintenance log and the absence of testimony from colleagues who might have performed the intervention are strong negative evidence. A colleague's contemporaneous account of an unlogged intervention would substantially raise this; absence of such testimony keeps it relatively low.

hypotheses.label: Post-day-10 data are systematically corrupted: readings are sign-inverted, unit-miscoded, or time-tagged to wrong dates
hypotheses.rationale: The negative cross-correlations between resonator and pendulum streams (resonator_lab ↔ pendulum_lab: −0.810; resonator_obs ↔ pendulum_obs: −0.798) could in principle arise from systematic sign inversion or unit mismatch in post-day-10 data. However, this hypothesis remains very low probability because the internal structure of correlations argues against simple corruption: (1) Within-instrument temporal structure (7-day autocorrelations 0.602–0.629) is preserved uniformly across all streams and would be anomalously preserved even under sign inversion, but the *magnitude* of autocorrelations would remain unaffected—this is consistent; (2) If post-day-10 data were sign-inverted, cross-correlations should flip sign relative to pre-day-10 baselines, but instead the within-type correlations are positive (both pendulums together, both resonators together) while cross-type correlations are negative—this would require inversion to affect only cross-type pairs, which is asymmetric and implausible; (3) The minimum value spacing (0.0001) is uniform across all instruments and periods, consistent with genuine precision measurement rather than miscoding; (4) Today's day-21 observations (events 699917–572285 for pendulum_lab, events 177120–634960 for resonator_obs) fall within ranges expected from post-shift means and show reasonable internal variation, not wildly off-scale or inverted polarity. Lowered from 0.08 to 0.04 because today's evidence reinforces internal consistency of the correlation structure across all four streams.

hypotheses.label: Seven-day operational or environmental cycle is the dominant unresolved anomaly; day-12 shift is secondary
hypotheses.rationale: The 7-day lag structure (pendulum_lab echo 0.602 at lag-2, pendulum_obs 0.629, resonator_lab 0.612, resonator_obs 0.617) is real and reproducible, suggesting a repeating operational or environmental cycle. However, this hypothesis ranks lowest because: (1) The 7-day cycle does not create strong cross-correlations between instruments at the 7-day lag; instead, correlations are dominated at 0-day lag (0.770–0.810), indicating the cycle is local to each instrument, not a shared environmental driver affecting all four in phase; (2) The day-12 level shift is far more statistically significant (|z| ≥ 9.87) than the magnitude of the 7-day cycle, which appears as a modest 0.5–0.6 autocorrelation within ongoing noise; (3) If the 7-day cycle were the primary driver, it should modulate all four instruments coherently, but instead the shift is directionally consistent within instrument type (both pendulums up, both resonators down), not across cycle phase; (4) The 7-day autocorrelation structure persists *after* the day-12 shift (post-shift n=66 for most streams), suggesting the cycle and the shift are independent phenomena, not confounded.
